papers.title: BaitBench: a comprehensive tool for building, as-sessing, and predicting outcomes for hybrid capture enrichment probes
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of hybridization capture sequencing, a powerful lab technique to isolate and characterize low-abundance samples from complex nucleic acid mixtures, relies heavily on creating a robust probe set. There are a variety of tools that design, evaluate, or simulate capture probes, however, these tools are often siloed and frequently difficult to use. To our knowledge there is no tool that connects all steps of the hybridization capture probe development and analysis process. Here we introduce BaitBench, a comprehensive tool to aid in the design, assessment, and simulation of target capture probes. BaitBench wraps or reimplements in Rust several current tools, and implements a thermodynamic model for simulating capture. Integrating steps allows us to track simulated reads through the whole process enabling us to report sources of false positives and reasons for false negatives. Easy to read output files and the ability to run via command line or GUI interfaces increases usability. We validated BaitBench against publicly available data and achieved a high correlation ({rho} = 0.916), demonstrating its accuracy and translation to real-world settings. Code is available at github.com/niel-infante/BaitBench, with installers for Mac and Windows available at github.com/niel-infante/BaitBench/releases.

papers.title: Alignment-Free k-mer Analysis Reveals Age-Associated k-mer Signals in Canine Buccal DNA and Cell-Free DNA
papers.abstract: Aging is associated with progressive molecular and cellular changes that alter chromatin organization, epigenetic regulation, and microbial community structure. While DNA methylation-based biomarkers have demonstrated age-prediction performance, the potential of alignment-free sequence analysis for detecting age-associated signals remains unexplored. We performed a k-mer-based analysis of whole-genome sequencing datasets from two canine cohorts: 1,187 buccal DNA samples and 100 cell-free DNA (cfDNA) samples. Age-associated k-mers were identified through correlation analysis, and sequence motifs and nucleotide composition patterns were characterized across both sample types. Ridge regression models were used to predict age from k-mer frequency profiles, and synthetic datasets were generated under biological compositional assumptions to evaluate potential drivers of the observed signals. Age-associated k-mer signals were identified in both buccal DNA and cfDNA, with substantially stronger patterns observed in buccal samples. Buccal-derived k-mers exhibited more pronounced motif patterns, stronger GC and AT enrichment trends, and improved age-prediction performance relative to cfDNA. Nucleotide enrichment trends differed between sample types, suggesting that distinct biological processes may contribute to age-associated sequence composition changes in buccal DNA and cfDNA. Simulation analyses successfully reproduced major enrichment trends observed empirically, and age-associated signals were largely preserved following restriction to read-start sequence composition. These findings demonstrate that alignment-free k-mer analysis can detect age-associated sequence composition signals in canine DNA and highlight its potential as a computationally efficient complementary approach for aging biomarker discovery.

papers.title: Multiscale Transcriptomic Architecture of the ALS Motor Cortex
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) exhibits marked clinical and molecular heterogeneity, but how this heterogeneity is organized within disease-relevant central nervous system regions remains incompletely understood. Because pooled cross-region analyses may confound regional variation with subtype structure, we focused on the motor cortex, a key site of ALS pathology, to resolve its internal transcriptomic organization. Using approximately 600 postmortem motor cortex transcriptomes from the Target ALS resource, we applied gene set variation analysis to generate sample-level pathway activity profiles and performed consensus clustering in pathway space. We identified seven reproducible ALS motor cortex subtypes characterized by distinct inflammatory, damage-response, metabolic, glial, and neuronal/synaptic programs. Donor-held-out projection recovered the seven subtype assignments with a mean balanced accuracy of 0.939, supporting the reproducibility of the pathway-defined subtype structure in unseen donors. Mapping these bulk-defined programs to an independent motor-cortex single-nucleus RNA-seq dataset revealed distinct cellular contexts, while cell-type marker adjustment showed that cellular differences contributed to, but did not fully account for, subtype-associated pathway variation. The seven subtypes also recapitulated major molecular programs reported in previous ALS subtype frameworks while resolving them into finer motor-cortex-specific states. Rather than forming isolated molecular classes, these subtypes occupied a structured pathway-space landscape with both discrete subtype-centered peaks and continuous biological gradients. Principal component analysis and representative pathway overlays defined a major axis from an upper inflammatory/damage region to a lower neuronal/metabolic/remodeling region, with C7 forming a neuronal/synaptic connector within the lower landscape. Co-expression network analysis further supported this multiscale organization, revealing family-level network backbones, subtype-specific modular refinements, and bridge-like rewiring. Metadata-informed analyses showed that this molecular architecture was not primarily organized by disease duration. Instead, the landscape was more clearly associated with clinical and genetic-background variables, including ALS/FTD family history and mutation-related signals. In particular, family-history-positive and C9orf72 repeat expansion-positive samples were more represented in the lower neuronal/metabolic/remodeling region, whereas family-history-negative samples and C9orf72-negative cases were more represented in the upper inflammatory/damage region. These findings support a model in which ALS motor cortex heterogeneity is organized as a multiscale transcriptomic architecture more closely associated with genetic-background variables than with disease duration. This framework provides a basis for subtype-aware biological comparison, future patient-stratification, biomarker, or therapeutic target-prioritization studies.

papers.title: Separating benchmark discrimination from experimental retrieval in synthetic-lethality prediction
papers.abstract: Degree-aware evaluation can expose sampling bias in synthetic-lethality prediction, but how should a model's degree-controlled benchmark score inform its use in experimental screening? We link fixed-prediction benchmark interventions to retrieval in measured experimental pools. Across five gene-disjoint folds, replacing Random test negatives with degree-matched negatives changed mean AUROC from 0.782 to 0.501 for SLMGAE, 0.721 to 0.502 for GCATSL, 0.656 to 0.492 for GRSMF, and 0.376 to 0.519 for SL2MF. The opposite movement of SL2MF shows that test composition can suppress as well as inflate discrimination. Crossed training-testing experiments and a three-seed diagnostic separated these changes from degeneration during matched GCATSL training. In four measured screens, the same Random-trained SLMGAE states retrieved 21 SPIDR hits in 198 selections, versus 8.00 expected under random ranking: a 2.62-fold enrichment despite near-chance matched-test AUROC (within-task Holm-adjusted p=0.0008). Comparable robust primary gains were not established in HAP1, a 27-cell-line compendium, or SCHEMATIC, where limited coverage and dependent observations constrain inference. A separate in-domain HAP1 control retrieved 11 hits versus 2.02 expected. These results establish an empirical dissociation between degree-controlled benchmark discrimination and experimental hit retrieval. A near-chance matched-test score can coexist with useful experimental prioritization. Our released evaluation suite makes both properties measurable from saved predictions, alongside checks of training viability and task coverage.

papers.title: iGEX: an interactive Gene EXpression exploration platform for the analysis of transcriptomic and proteomic datasets
papers.abstract: High-throughput transcriptomic and proteomic studies have generated a rapidly expanding collection of publicly available datasets. However, extracting biological insight from these resources often requires researchers to repeatedly download, reformat, integrate and analyse individual files using specialised tools. This process is time-consuming and often requires coding expertise. Here, we present iGEX, an interactive exploration platform that can incorporate publicly available and user-generated transcriptomic and proteomic datasets into a single visual workspace to simplify the analysis of multiple transcripts and/or proteins across numerous datasets. iGEX enables researchers to select gene/protein targets and experiments and compare expression patterns across biological conditions and experiments. User-generated data can be examined alongside numerous public resources such as EMBL-EBI Expression Atlas, Bgee, and PaxDb to determine whether any observed patterns are evident across experiments, species or experimental contexts. Users can visualise and move directly between data tables, principal component analysis, expression and correlation heatmaps, hierarchical clustering and volcano plots, all of which are editable and downloadable.

papers.title: Digital twins forecast individual immune trajectories
papers.abstract: The human immune system differs markedly between individuals and changes in response to infection, vaccination and treatment. AI virtual cells are being built to simulate cellular responses to perturbation. Yet these models, like most immune-response predictors, describe each person by a single pre-challenge measurement and forecast change from patterns pooled across people. Digital twins, updated with every new observation of an individual, could forecast how that person's immune state changes. Here we present ImmuneTwins, which builds these twins from single-cell profiles by personalizing a shared virtual-cell model with each individual's observations. In two external populations, ImmuneTwins reduced immune-age error by 32% and 42% relative to the best existing method. During repeated influenza vaccination, its twins predicted the direction of immune-cell change 35% more accurately than the best published method, and their error fell by 27% as observations accumulated. The twins revealed that immune cells and plasma proteins recover about half their deviation from a persistent personal reference within 90 days, whereas response size varies between challenges. They further localized B-cell remodelling in exceptional longevity and anticipated patient-specific immune trajectories during myeloma treatment. These results establish virtual-cell digital twins for forecasting individual immune change and identifying each person's characteristic immune features.

papers.title: Does a map-level insulation constraint improve sequence-based prediction of 3D genome folding? A Stage 1 Registered Report with a reverse-complement-equivariant state-space model (HiFold-Mamba)
papers.abstract: Background. Sequence-to-contact-map models are trained with pixel-wise losses, although the features of interest (insulation, domain boundaries, loops) are summaries of the map. Insulationbased losses help Hi-C resolution enhancement. No pre-specified test has asked whether they improve sequence-based prediction, judged against annotations independent of the training data. Proposed study. HiFold-Mamba predicts 448 x 448 maps at 2,048 bp from 1,048,576 bp of DNA on the DNALongBench contact-map task. Every component is reverse-complement-equivariant: convolutional tower, bidirectional Mamba blocks, multi-scale mixer and symmetric pairwise head. We pre-register three hypotheses: >> H1: it exceeds each of three trained baselines (reproduced Akita, a parameter-matched Transformer and a parameter-matched CNN) by [≥]0.01 stratum-adjusted correlation (SCC). >> H2: an insulation and boundary loss, computed from the predicted map with the operator used on the observed map, improves boundary AUROC and loop AP against independent 4DN boundary calls and ENCODE CTCF ChIA-PET loops, at equal training steps and without loss of SCC. >> H3: pretraining plus few-shot adaptation beats training from scratch on four held-out cell lines.Tests use a paired bootstrap over 237 one-megabase test blocks (one-sided = 0.025). Pilot data. >> Verification. The benchmark target, the window coordinates and the networks equivariance were verified. >> Locus-shared reference. Copying other cell lines measured maps at the same locus matches published Akita on the benchmarks SCC (0.227 vs. 0.230). >> SCC weightings. Two weightings in common use weight distance strata in opposite directions and agree only moderately ({rho} = 0.54). >> Comparison rule. In simulations calibrated on the pilot data, a per-block-best comparison against several baselines has no power. We therefore test against each baseline, which gives [≥] 90 % power at a true gain of 0.02 when between-model correlation is [≥] 0.95. >> H2 positive control. On validation windows, observed maps recover the independent boundaries (AUROC 0.61 - 0.91) and loops (0.86 - 0.90). This fixed the insulation window and showed that these annotations are largely shared across cell types.

papers.title: GaussF: An Unbiased Gaussian Framework for High-Precision Transcript Quantification with a Programmable Self-Benchmark Model
papers.abstract: Short-read RNA sequencing has revolutionized transcriptome analysis, but accurate isoform-level quantification faces substantial challenges from overlapping sequences among complex isoforms and inherent sequencing biases, leading to uneven coverage. Current alignment-based and alignment-free methods, while valuable, largely rely on empirical, data-derived factors for bias correction and isoform resolution. This dependency limits their capacity to fully capture the intricate spectrum of sequencing data. We introduce GaussF, a novel alignment-free methodology specifically designed for precise isoform quantification by directly addressing these biases and the isoform recognition problem without relying on empirical data. GaussF is predicated on the observation that k-mer counts categorized by GC content across a natural transcript exhibit an intrinsic Gaussian distribution. It establishes a transcript-specific self-benchmarking workflow utilizing a theoretical Gaussian cumulative distribution function (CDF). Crucially, the parameters defining this CDF are derived independently of any empirical sequencing data. This parameter-fixed theoretical CDF serves as an unbiased benchmark, capturing only the genuine contribution of abundance while systematically excluding all bias-related data. To improve isoform resolution despite shared regions, GaussF characterizes isoforms through identifying minimal-shared regions and restructures the k-mer reference accordingly. This approach simplifies complexity and enhances accuracy. Rigorous validation using artificial and real RNA samples, alongside comparative analysis with leading quantification tools like Kallisto, Salmon, Cufflinks, StringTie, and RSEM, demonstrates GaussF's superior performance in accurate isoform detection and quantification. GaussF is available on GitHub and PyPI, representing a significant advancement in RNA-seq analysis.

papers.title: Network analysis reveals converging molecular mechanisms in genetic epilepsies
papers.abstract: Background: Rare genetic epilepsies are often difficult to diagnose and treat. They can arise from changes in many different genes, and the molecular basis linking these changes to epilepsy remains poorly understood. This complexity makes it difficult to select effective treatments and develop new therapies, leaving many patients with poorly controlled seizures and reduced quality of life Methods: To address this gap, we first identified epilepsy-associated genes and conducted a network-based analysis of biomolecular interactions in genetic epilepsy to identify converging pathways with high translational relevance and potential therapeutic targets. To run the analysis, we constructed a human brain-specific molecular interaction network by integrating all human pathways from the WikiPathways database. HotNet2 was then applied to identify highly perturbed clusters through evidence-based weight diffusion of EAGs in the human brain network. Results: We identified 2,496 epilepsy-associated genes (EAGs) from multiple resources. These genes encode coding for metabolite interconversion enzymes (20%), transporters (15%), and protein-modifying enzymes (11%). Furthermore, the network analysis identified 19 subnetworks with more than two nodes and 125 unique genes. Gene enrichment analysis revealed convergence of processes including action potential, synaptic function, nervous system development, TOR signaling, cilium organization, DNA repair, and cell fate specification. We identified 44 first-order neighbors connecting the subnetworks. By integrating drug-target interactions from DrugBank using CyTargetLinker, we highlighted potential therapeutic targets within the S4 subnetwork, associated with cerebral cortex development, as well as CREB1, a connector between subnetworks. Conclusion: Network analysis organized heterogeneous epilepsy-associated genes into biologically related subnetworks and generated hypotheses for further research.

papers.title: Fox: Predicting rates of host-symbiont co-evolution events with association-aware attention
papers.abstract: Motivation: Hosts and their symbionts share a history of associations in which lineages cospeciate, switch hosts, duplicate, or are lost. Quantifying the relative frequencies of these four events is a central goal of cophylogenetics, but existing tools typically require a fully resolved, correctly rooted host tree, often alongside a symbiont tree, propagating tree-inference errors into the reconciliation and scaling poorly to large systems. Results: We introduce Fox, a transformer neural network architecture that infers the relative frequencies of the four cophylogenetic events directly from a pair of host and symbiont multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) and their sequence mapping, with no tree-reconstruction or reconciliation step. Fox is trained under a simulation-based inference scheme: it learns event frequencies from alignments generated by a coevolutionary process, paying its computational cost once at training time and processing any new system in a single forward pass. On held-out data from its training simulator, Fox recovers event frequencies accurately and with near-zero bias. On additional synthetic data from an independent cophylogeny simulator, its error roughly doubled, but is still very low allowing to track the true frequencies. Most importantly, when compared to the Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC)-based method AmoCoala on these data, it reduces mean absolute error by 45-76% for cospeciations, host switches and duplications and shows similar error for losses, while running more than three orders of magnitude faster. Applied to the empirical cockroach-Blattabacterium system, Fox recovers the expected cospeciation-dominated profile, showing that behaviour learned on simulated data transfers to real sequences. These results confirm that the coevolutionary signal usually extracted from trees can be read directly, accurately, and fast in the alignments themselves

papers.title: Assembly of minimally fragmented metagenomic pangenome graphs
papers.abstract: Pangenome variation graphs are a powerful tool for representing genetic diversity within and across populations. For comparative and evolutionary genomic analyses leveraging these graph-based structures, it is important that graph topology reflects the underlying phylogenetic and genetic similarities of the genomes embedded within the graph. However, in metagenomic settings these approaches often produce highly fragmented multi-component graphs, hindering comparisons of genomes embedded across different components. This challenge is particularly pronounced for hypervariable viral families like Anelloviridae, whose short circular genomes frustrate existing variation graph construction methods. We present PANIMaSTA (Progressive Average Nucleotide Identity and Maximum Spanning Tree-Based Assembly), a workflow to construct minimally fragmented metagenomic pangenome sequence variation graphs through progressive assembly. The order in which the genomes are incorporated into the graph is informed by a maximum spanning tree (MST) inferred from an all-to-all genome similarity matrix comprised of pairwise Anelloviridae average nucleotide identities (ANI). Applied to over 5,200 diverse Anelloviridae genomes, we construct a sequence variation graph whose graph topology reflects the global genome similarities observed across the ANI matrix. PANIMaSTA constructs minimally fragmented metagenomic pangenome sequence variation graphs that are not achievable with existing methods suitable for similarity-aware sequence-to-graph mapping and downstream genetic analyses across highly diverse genomes.

papers.title: Predicting Differential Protein-Protein Interactions
papers.abstract: Motivation Analysis of context-specific protein-protein interactions (PPIs) provides deeper insight into protein function, revealing how cellular pathway components interact in certain perturbation conditions. However, identifying such interactions experimentally often requires combining affinity purification with mass spectrometry, proving costly and time-consuming. On the other hand, it has been shown that an increase in protein abundance does not always correspond to an increase in protein interaction, making it an unsuitable surrogate for interaction studies. Results To address this, a random forest model was created using PPI-specific MINT embeddings and condition-specific mass spectrometry protein abundance information to predict differential interactions across two experimental conditions. The model was trained and tested on validated context-specific PPIs from eight distinct cell-lines, demonstrating proficiency in predicting differential PPIs for both novel proteins and cell lines. To our knowledge, we provide the first computational model that predicts differential PPIs between experimental conditions. Availability and implementation The code is available on GitHub and backed up on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23758127). The model is freely available on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23757927).

papers.title: Protein co-scientist aided simulations of the structural and functional impact of O-GlcNAc Transferase TPR domain deletions and amino acid substitutions associated with X-Linked Intellectual Disability
papers.abstract: O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) is an essential glycosyltransferase that regulates cellular processes through the addition of O-linked {beta}-N-acetyglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) to target proteins. Substrate recognition and protein-protein interactions are mediated by the tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain, yet the contributions of individual TPR repeats to structural stability and function remain poorly understood. Here, we employed an integrated computational framework combining an AI protein co-scientist, Speak to a Protein, which incorporates Boltz-2 for structure prediction and rDock for ligand binding evaluation, with external tools including AlphaFold3 for more advanced structure prediction and the HDOCK server for protein-protein docking. This framework was used to investigate how deletions of TPR domains and disease-associated amino acid substitutions within the TPR domain affect OGT structure and function. Five synthetic truncation OGT isoforms, thirteen single-TPR deletion variants, and five X-linked intellectual disability (XLID)-associated amino acid substitutions were modeled and aligned to wild-type OGT for comparison. Structural perturbations were quantified using backbone root mean square deviation (RMSD), while functional effects were assessed through docking analyses with UDP-GlcNAc, Host Cell Factor 1 (HCF1), and Tet methylcytosine dioxygenase 1 (TET1). Variation in TPR length altered global protein structure and induced long-range conformational changes within the catalytic domain despite no sequence modifications in that region. Single TPR deletions showed that individual repeats contribute unequally to structural stability, with deletions in mid-to-late TPR domains producing the largest structural disruptions. Disease-associated amino acid substitutions also generated conformational changes and reduced predicted ligand binding, consistent with known reductions in enzymatic activity in XLID. Protein-protein docking analyses demonstrated substrate-specific effects, as domain deletion and amino acid substitution variants of OGT had different interactions with TET1 and HCF1. Collectively, these findings identify the TPR domain as a regulatory domain that governs structure, ligand recognition, and protein interactions. More broadly, this work demonstrates how the integration of a protein co-scientist with protein structure modeling tools can be used to predict the structural and functional consequences of domain deletions or natural amino acid variants.

papers.title: Carrier-Limited Release Risk in Electrospun Nanofibers for Regenerative Endodontics: Constraint Discovery from 25 Formulations
papers.abstract: Regenerative endodontics needs an intracanal carrier that keeps disinfecting across a dressing interval that clinicians schedule at one to four weeks, without harming the stem cells that rebuild the pulp. We ask what one completed 25-formulation electrospinning campaign of poly(vinylpyrrolidone) (PVP) fibers carrying metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, minocycline and Ca(OH)2 can decide, and use machine learning for constraint discovery and decision support rather than as a new predictor. After an audit against the source thesis, logistic regression predicts fine-fiber formation at 96% leave-one-out accuracy, but a one-threshold rule does as well, the gain over the 80% majority baseline is not significant (exact McNemar p = 0.125), and accuracy falls to 84% when mixture loading is encoded per component. Diameter models interpolate within formulation families (ridge MAE 193 nm, 95% CI 96 to 317 nm) and fail across them (R^2 < 0). Because the campaign never measured release, we assemble a same-drug, cross-carrier evidence table: 17 bounded metronidazole and ciprofloxacin observations from seven studies, with two-sided censoring. Water-soluble carriers (PVP, PVA) completed release within 80 h (PVP within 8 h); no water-insoluble monolithic carrier reached 90% within its observation window, releasing 1.5 to 50%; both within-study comparisons separate at matched loading; and blend, core-shell and thick-mat architectures released over 3 to 28 days. The PVP mats therefore carry a carrier-limited release risk, not a proven ceiling, and one dissolution experiment can confirm or overturn it. A censoring-aware screen keeps three necessarily and one possibly nondominated formulation, and fixed-budget replays show that uncertainty sampling finds failed formulations sooner, except the one it is confidently wrong about.

papers.title: Arena3D 3.0: a web server for exploring, analyzing, annotating and sharing multilayered networks in 3D
papers.abstract: Multilayer networks describe biological entities linked by several kinds of relation or measured under several conditions. Arena3D 3.0, a complete reimplementation of Arena3Dweb, gives each layer its own place in an interactive 3D scene. Networks are uploaded or imported from STRING, IntAct, OmniPath, NDEx, Reactome and the Gene Ontology. Twelve layouts, seven in 3D, are available, and node copies can be aligned across layers. Layers are drawn as floors or 3D containers in thirteen arrangements, including 3D hive plots. Communities and annotated groups can be laid out apart and outlined as hulls or fog clouds, and edges can be bundled. Analyses cover node and multilayer metrics, distributions and perturbation, with chord, Sankey, heatmap, UpSet and UMAP views. Networks go to Cytoscape, Gephi Lite, NORMA and JBrowse 2, gene lists to Flame, and a REST API gives programmatic access. Arena3D 3.0 is free at www.arena3d.org without login.

papers.title: IG-28 enables identification and quantification of high-confidence isoforms from large bulk and single-cell full-length cDNA datasets
papers.abstract: The technology to sequence full-length transcriptomes from bulk and single-cell samples has rapidly advanced. As a result, full-length cDNA datasets now reach billions of reads in size which is beyond the capability of most established isoform identification tools. Here, we introduce IG-28 which addresses this challenge with its capability to process and analyze large fl-cDNA datasets fast and using minimal computational resources. In contrast to its predecessor Mandalorion, IG-28 is not limited to bulk fl-cDNA but is capable of parsing, processing, and analyzing single-cell fl-cDNA datasets. It does so in a lightweight, flexible manner, integrating seamlessly with established scRNA-seq analysis workflows. We benchmarked IG-28 against a variety of established and new isoform identification tools using several bulk and a complex single-cell fl-cDNA dataset and found that IG-28 consistently outperformed the other tools by identifying high-confidence public isoforms.

papers.title: Interpreting Graph Neural Networks for Antibacterial Drug Repurposing against Acinetobacter baumannii
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in Acinetobacter baumannii, whose carbapenem-resistant strains are classified by the World Health Organization as a critical priority, has motivated machine-learning screens for new antibacterials, but translating predictions into chemical hypotheses requires evaluating the molecular features on which a model relies. A graph neural network ensemble achieves competitive predictive performance against a descriptor-augmented reference model on the same antibacterial screen while using only atom features and connectivity, allowing interpretation to focus on the molecular graph without a separate input of handcrafted descriptors. The atom-level explanations identify features supporting the model's activity predictions under perturbation and restoration, while comparisons with equally sized perturbations within each molecule distinguish piperazine as the most consistently supported recurring contributor to predicted activity. Prospective screening of the Drug Repurposing Hub followed by developability and safety assessment yields a ranked shortlist for experimental follow-up and leads to testing of CE3F4, which reduced A. baumannii growth by 57% at 0.25 mM in a preliminary assay with a non-monotonic concentration--response profile.

papers.title: Agentic Discovery Transfer Enables Cross-Cancer Discovery at Scale
papers.abstract: Cancer research generates tens of thousands of studies each year, yet whether a published finding holds in another cancer type or patient population is rarely tested, because doing so is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. We define this task as discovery transfer and present SMART, a multi-agent large language model framework for discovery transfer in single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies. Given a source manuscript and a target scRNA-seq dataset, SMART extracts major clinical and mechanistic findings, generates and executes analyses for the testable findings, and reports which findings transfer and suggests follow-up. Applied to 121 studies across six cancer types, SMART identified findings that transfer across cancers, including a lung cancer prognostic signature that we confirmed to be associated with survival in liver cancer, pancreatic cancer and pleural mesothelioma. SMART also generated new mechanistic hypotheses, demonstrating how agentic discovery transfer can extend published findings beyond their original setting.

papers.title: Transcriptomic similarity guides source selection beyond tissue lineage
papers.abstract: Perturbational and pharmacogenomic maps remain incomplete across cellular contexts, leaving a practical source-selection question before response prediction: which measured context should inform an unmeasured target? We tested whether baseline transcriptomic similarity ranks candidate sources for held-out targets, separating source ranking from aggregation and transfer-uncertainty decisions. Similarity tracked matched-response concordance in LINCS and GSE306429; selected-source utility exceeded random expectation in GSE306429 ({Delta}U = 0.034; P = 0.002) and in exact-time-matched MIX-Seq tasks ({Delta}U = 0.046). In the full GDSC2 analysis, the drug-balanced ranking effect was 0.359 (95% CI, 0.337-0.383). In a lineage-restricted analysis of the same eligible subset, within-tissue ranking remained positive at 0.130 (95% CI, 0.119-0.141), retaining 35.8% of the same-subset global effect (0.363; 95% CI, 0.342-0.386). Global transcriptomic top-1 selection exceeded tissue-matched random selection by 0.154 (95% CI, 0.143-0.164). Thus, baseline similarity adds source-ranking information after tissue matching in the evaluated setting, while ranking alone does not resolve whether to aggregate sources or how to quantify transfer uncertainty.

papers.title: Efficient biological design via genomic in-context learning
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL), the ability to perform new tasks from a few examples supplied in a prompt, is a defining emergent capability of large language models. Here, we show that ICL emerges in the genome language model Evo 2 and enables biological design. With as few as four examples in the prompt and no additional training, Evo 2 generates realistic metal-binding proteins, de novo antibodies, protein-RNA systems, and entire bacteriophage genomes. For {Phi}X174-like bacteriophage design, ICL surpasses previously fine-tuned models on computational measures of design quality and diversity. Beyond {Phi}X174, conditioning the model with different phage prompts enables us to efficiently design MS2 and M13 genomes in silico without fine-tuning. Iteratively updating the prompt with newly generated phage genomes, which we refer to as genomic chain-of-thought, further improves the diversity of designs while maintaining quality metrics. Paired with an inference engine that accelerates generation up to 35-fold and extends practicable context to a megabase, these results establish ICL as a versatile and efficient paradigm for biological sequence design.

papers.title: Joint localization and testing reveals spatial context of differential expression
papers.abstract: Multi-subject spatial transcriptomics is increasingly used to identify molecular differences across individuals and conditions while resolving where in tissue those differences occur. Yet subject-level differential expression (DE) analyses commonly require spatial regions to be specified in advance, separating localization from testing. Here we present SpaceDX, a framework that uses gene-specific attention-based spatial weighting to jointly test differential expression and localize the spatial expression patterns contributing to these associations. In simulations, SpaceDX outperforms cluster-based DE methods when differential expression does not align with predefined spatial boundaries. Across two multi-subject mouse brain datasets, SpaceDX detected 45.8% more DE genes than regional DESeq2 pseudobulk in a chronic stress model, while in an Alzheimer's disease model combining SpaceDX with DESeq2 increased discovery by 19.1% relative to DESeq2 alone. Across both datasets, the learned maps provided spatial context for condition-associated expression signals in addition to gene-level significance. In the chronic stress model, for example, oligodendrocyte- and myelin-associated genes showed shared localization to corresponding brain structures. Together, these results show that the spatial context of differential expression can be inferred jointly with gene-level associations, recovering signals obscured by regional aggregation without requiring the relevant tissue context to be defined in advance.

papers.title: Scooby-2: fine-tuning AlphaGenome for single-cell genomic track prediction
papers.abstract: Sequence-to-function models predict genomic tracks from DNA sequence. AlphaGenome has been shown to outperform previous models, including Borzoi, on most track-prediction and variant-effect benchmarks. However, like its predecessors, it predicts tracks only for predefined, mostly bulk-derived cell types and tissues. While Scooby has extended Borzoi to single-cell resolution, a single-cell adaptation of AlphaGenome is still lacking. We present Scooby-2, which combines AlphaGenome with a cell-specific decoder to predict single-cell RNA-seq coverage and chromatin-accessibility genomic tracks from DNA sequence. The package provides the implementation, the parameter-efficient fine-tuning setup, the training pipeline and inference scripts. When evaluated on the NeurIPS bone marrow single-cell dataset, Scooby-2 achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.56 when predicting cell-type-specific gene expression differences, compared with 0.53 for Scooby. When using the distilled AlphaGenome backbone, variant effect prediction concordance of fine-mapped eQTLs from the OneK1K cohort improved from 0.37 to 0.47 Spearman's rank correlation across all associations, an improvement consistent with that of AlphaGenome over Borzoi itself.

papers.title: mito-overview: a mitochondrial report software
papers.abstract: Interpreting mitochondrial DNA variation requires relating allele representation and genomic annotation to the sequencing evidence available for each sample. We developed mito-overview to integrate mitochondrial coverage, candidate allele fractions, genomic annotations and long read co-occurrence in mitochondrial genomic reports. Analysis of a subset of public GM12878 long read data from Vandiver and colleagues Cas9 enrichment study of full-length mitochondrial genomes (SRR18110025) identified 16 candidate variants. Among these candidates, co-occurrence analysis showed that m.8860A>G and m.14831G>A occurred together in all 366 jointly callable query names, demonstrating how mito-overview extends individual allele measurements to quantify shared read support between mitochondrial sites. Analysis of public GM11906 short read data (GSE142741), pooled from three single-cell ATAC-seq libraries, recovered the previously characterized disease-associated m.8344A>G variant in MT-TK at an alternate allele fraction of 72.1% (740 of 1,027 callable observations). The recovered variant identity and MT-TK assignment agree with Lareau and colleagues original study, providing a disease-relevant example of mito-overview combined candidate detection and genomic annotation. We also examined ONT data from blood, fibroblast and muscle of one patient using a separate internal workflow. Heteroplasmy was estimated from alternate allele fractions calculated separately for each tissue. The respective analyses yielded 90, 52 and 60 candidates, with 19 candidate identities shared across all three lists. For these shared candidates, the tissue-specific estimates enabled examination of both variant presence and allele representation across the sampled tissues, illustrating the application of mitochondrial genomic reports to heteroplasmy assessment in disease research. By combining candidate identification with allele measurements, genomic annotations and shared read support, mito-overview enables researchers to examine which variants are observed, their representation within a sample and their co-occurrence with other mitochondrial alleles. These complementary measurements support the selection and characterization of candidate variants for further study in mitochondrial disease research.

papers.title: Ground-truth evaluation of sparse autoencoder features on spatial, single-cell and language-model embeddings
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are increasingly used to extract interpretable features from the embeddings of biological foundation models. Because SAEs trained with different random seeds learn different features, reproducibility across seeds has become a common test of whether these features can be trusted. We asked whether reproducible features are also meaningful, using embeddings whose concepts are known: five spatial transcriptomics embeddings of two colorectal cancer sections and Geneformer embeddings of single-cell RNA profiles, with cell lineages as concepts; synthetic data with planted cell states; and the residual stream of a small language model, with token classes as concepts. Varimax rotations of the same embeddings were almost perfectly reproducible, yet rotation features (PCA, varimax and ICA) covered at most three of seven lineages and three of eight token classes. Single SAE fits showed the opposite profile: they covered most concepts with purer gene programs but reproduced only 27-46% of their features. A consensus over five SAE fits combined the two strengths. It was reproducible (78-98% across sources) and as pure as single fits: 11-40% of its features carried marker genes of another lineage, against 44-70% for varimax. Against the strongest baseline, varimax sparsified to the SAE's sparsity, the consensus covered as many concepts on PCA and Geneformer embeddings and more on learned spatial and text embeddings. The consensus also had costs. It covered fewer lineages than single fits and, like all SAEs, missed weak planted states that rotations recovered; neither a longer single fit nor a second SAE trained on the consensus residual recovered what it discarded. Reproducibility alone therefore ranks features poorly: SAE features should be reported with the number of known concepts they cover and the purity of their gene programs, against a rotation of the same embedding sparsified to the SAE's sparsity.

papers.title: Evaluation of Cross-slice Imputation for Spatial Proteomics
papers.abstract: Spatial single-cell protein profiling is at the forefront of translational medicine research efforts that try to decipher tissue heterogeneity. However, existing experimental approaches are limited in the number of biomarkers that they measure. This has motivated extensive research into the problem of protein imputation, where proteins or biomarkers not directly measured in a given slice of biopsy tissue are learned from those measured. In this work, we focus on the specific problem of cross-slice protein imputation (CSPI). In the CSPI problem, two sets of biomarker expressions at the single-cell level are known for physically adjacent slices of tissue. Each slice has its own known set of biomarkers, which overlaps with but does not subsume that of the adjacent. For each slice, we wish to learn the expressions of the proteins unique to the adjacent. Existing literature for protein imputation methodologies can be grouped in two categories: learning-based and alignment-based approaches. Learning-based approaches do not account for spatial and structural similarities between the training and the target sets. Alignment based approaches aim to determine an association between cells in adjacent slices, but without the explicit goal of using this alignment for imputation. In this work, we evaluate several methods from both categories and their adaptability to the cross-slice protein imputation problem. We provide a statistical analysis of all methods' performance under varying conditions of implementation. We find that learning-based methods significantly outperform alignment-based methods at the task of cross-slice protein imputation, with the latter more suited to the task of inter-slice interpolation or 3D tissue reconstruction. Moreover, inter-patient imputation is far less accurate than intra-patient imputation for all methods evaluated.

papers.title: CellMethMarker provides an integrated database of human cell- and tissue-type-specific DNA methylation markers
papers.abstract: Cell- and tissue-type-specific DNA methylation markers provide epigenetic signatures of cellular identity and are widely used to infer cellular origin from bulk and single-cell methylomes. Existing resources mainly emphasize disease-associated biomarkers, methylome atlases, genomic annotations or RNA-based cell markers, leaving an unmet need for an integrated region-level resource dedicated to such markers. Here we present CellMethMarker (http://gu-zhanglab.hfcas.ac.cn/CellMethMarker), a curated database integrating 347,514 de novo markers derived from uniformly processed whole-genome and reduced-representation bisulfite sequencing datasets, 2,203,507 literature-derived marker records and harmonized metadata for 2,810 samples. CellMethMarker enables cell- and tissue-centered marker retrieval, coordinate-based search, genome-browser visualization, interactive methylation analysis and data download. In an independent single-cell methylome atlas, these markers recover the expected cell-type-associated methylation patterns, and a platform-matched reference built from them lowers the mean deconvolution error from 0.365 to 0.144. CellMethMarker therefore links region-level DNA methylation variation to cellular identity and supports methylome-based cell-type annotation and deconvolution.

papers.title: Multi-resolution humanness scoring of antibodies via a region-isolated language model
papers.abstract: Antibodies recognized as foreign can elicit anti-drug antibodies that compromise efficacy and safety, making humanness scoring, estimating how human-like a sequence appears, an early, repeated step in antibody development. Widely used scores reduce a variable domain to a single framework-dominated number, leaving the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) grafted during humanization, diversified by generative models weakly supervised and rarely audited. Here we introduce IgScope, a 23-million-parameter antibody language model trained from scratch that scores humanness at chain, IMGT-region, and residue resolution; a region-isolated attention module confines attention to within-region pairs, and chimeric-sequence training supplies region-level supervision. On 2.38 million held-out chains, masking all framework tokens leaves CDR accuracy unchanged, and back-mutated murine residues in human frameworks are detected at 93.4% accuracy. At chain level, IgScope matches the strongest published correlation with clinical anti-drug-antibody incidence (r = 0.567, n = 217) and outperforms a same-protocol recomputation. Region-level scoring exposes what chain-level scoring conceals: antibodies designed de novo by four generative models pass whole-chain humanness (0.966-0.988), while their CDRs score far below natural (P < 1e-30) in every chain class. Quality control turns the same resolution to the mirror-image question: in humanized-mouse platforms, whose domains are human by design, IgScope scores the domain as human and, in HUGO-Nano chimeric VHHs, isolates only the FR2 signal of four camelid hallmark residues deliberately retained to stabilize the VHH. IgScope gives antibody humanization a verified foundation and generative design an audit.

papers.title: NK-RCPP: a receptor-conditioned computational workflow for prioritizing neurokinin-receptor peptide candidates
papers.abstract: Prioritizing peptides for closely related G protein-coupled receptors requires comparing target-directed scores with evidence from other structural contexts. We applied the Neurokinin Receptor-Conditioned Peptide Prioritization workflow (NK-RCPP) to 96 generated candidates for neurokinin receptors NK1R, NK2R and NK3R. The retrospective analysis combined receptor-matched on-target REF15 scores with 4,518 paired structural-neighbour comparisons covering 82 candidates. Lower on-target scores than the matched controls were observed for 14/32 NK1R, 23/32 NK2R and 6/32 NK3R candidates. Adding the neighbour-score criterion retained 16 of the 33 evaluable on-target-favoured candidates, reducing that pool by 51.5%. At matched receptor-specific shortlist sizes, half of the candidate identities differed from on-target-only selection. NK2R-04 and NK2R-19 remained selected at the higher neighbour-fraction threshold of 0.75. Fourteen NK2R candidates lacked neighbour summaries, leaving their joint-rule status unresolved. Sequence-frequency and embedding analyses described the candidates within a 1,048-peptide comparison space, and an exploratory 10-peptide NK2R comparison showed differences in standardized scores with uncertain score-potency agreement. These findings show how paired structural-neighbour scoring and threshold choice shape candidate selection within a receptor family. The resulting shortlist provides a defined set for testing whether joint prioritization enriches for active, receptor-preferred peptides.

papers.title: Single-Nucleus Profiling Reveals Neuronal Metabolic Collapse During the Transition to Alzheimer's Disease Dementia
papers.abstract: Current Alzheimer's disease (AD) neuropathological metrics, including Thal phasing, and Braak staging, often do not accurately predict cognitive status: many cognitively resilient individuals have substantial pathological burdens, whereas some patients with dementia show minimal classical AD pathology. Here, we addressed this discrepancy by investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying AD dementia using single-nucleus RNA-sequencing and single-nucleus multiome datasets. To eliminate cross-modality scaling artifacts and compositional biases inherent in neurodegenerative tissues, we normalized the datasets using our novel framework, bypassing scaling issues of conventional methods that may obscure critical biological signals of interest. We identified neuron-specific suppression of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes and their upstream mitochondrial biogenesis signaling (MBS) as primary drivers of clinical dementia. By integrating multi-omic quantitative trait loci, genome-wide association studies, and epigenomic profiles, we delineated genetic and epigenetic changes underlying MBS suppression. This study provides a systematic genomic framework for understanding the mechanisms of cognitive resilience.

papers.title: Reference normalizations of Effort-To-Compress across length, alphabet size, and composition
papers.abstract: Comparing finite symbolic complexity requires an explicit reference. Effort-To-Compress (ETC) counts the recursive pair substitutions needed to reduce a symbolic sequence to a constant. Its conventional normalization with L - 1 leaves systematic dependence on sequence length L and alphabet size k, confounding comparisons across datasets. We derive certified lower bounds for ETC and show that, for L [≥] k [≥] 2, the ceiling L - 1 is attainable if and only if L [≤] k2 + k + 1. For fixed k [≥] 2, the global ensemble mean and maximum ETC grow as {Theta}k(L/ logk L) as L [->] {infty}. These support two normalized ETC coordinates. Global-ensemble normalized ETC (nETC) maps a certified lower bound to zero and the uniform ensemble mean at the same L and k to one. Composition-conditioned normalized ETC (cETC) uses corresponding references restricted to the observed symbol composition. In Potts chains, nETC substantially reduced dependence on length and alphabet size. cETC further reduced differences associated with unequal symbol frequencies, while retaining sensitivity to temporal dependence. In human chromosome 22, the exploratory predictor nETC - cETC outperformed LZ76 in distinguishing CpG islands and long interspersed nuclear elements from genomic background with AUROC of 0.947 and 0.848. Matched references therefore enable interpretable comparisons of symbolic complexity across sequence lengths, alphabet sizes, and compositions.
